core: What marketing ethics is: the working definition — principles of right conduct (honesty, responsibility, fairness) applied to marketing decisions — attributed to the AMA Statement of Ethics and OpenStax Principles of Marketing 5.7

Truthfulness: claims must be honest — the FTC standard that advertising must be truthful, not misleading, and evidence-backed, enforced in every medium; the FTC Endorsement Guides (disclose paid connections; testimonials reflect typical results)

Fairness: no exploiting vulnerable groups — children (persuasive intent), older adults (health claims), low-income consumers (costly credit); the AMA equity value; one original fictional example (QuickBridge loan app)
The gray zones: persuasion vs manipulation (the AMA honesty value rejects manipulation and coercion) and privacy vs personalization (FTC privacy role; original Harbor Books example)
The legal floor vs the ethical ceiling: law sets the minimum; the AMA statement asks marketers to follow all applicable laws and exceed legal standards where it matters
Ethics and trust: ethical marketing builds durable trust; branding referenced only as a sibling topic
The honest framing: ethics is the cost of staying in business long
supporting: The FTC's enforcement role: prevents anticompetitive, deceptive, and unfair business practices (About the FTC)
The FTC as the chief federal privacy agency since the 1970s (Protecting Consumer Privacy and Security topic page)
FTC business guidance: claims in advertisements must be truthful, cannot be deceptive or unfair, and must be evidence-based
outOfScope: Advertising mechanics, media, and campaign planning (sibling topic: advertising)
Consumer behavior and buying-decision psychology (sibling topic: consumer-behavior)
Ethical theory depth and moral-philosophy frameworks (owned by the philosophy subject)
Specific FTC cases, penalties, and enforcement histories
Policy positions on specific industries such as payday lending regulation

claims.claim: Marketing ethics is the application of principles of right conduct — honesty, responsibility, and fairness — to marketing decisions; the American Marketing Association's Statement of Ethics is the profession's best-known statement of those standards.
Under U.S. federal law, advertisements must be truthful and not misleading, and claims must be backed by evidence; the FTC enforces this standard in every medium.

The FTC's Endorsement Guides require endorsements to be truthful and not misleading; paid or otherwise material connections must be disclosed, and testimonials must reflect what consumers can generally expect.

Fairness in marketing includes not exploiting vulnerable groups: children under about seven or eight cannot yet distinguish an ad's persuasive intent, and older adults and low-income consumers are commonly targeted with health claims and costly credit.
The AMA Statement of Ethics calls on marketers to do no harm, to reject manipulation and coercion, to be transparent, and to recognize the needs of vulnerable market segments.

The law sets the minimum standard; the AMA Statement of Ethics asks marketers to adhere to all applicable laws at a minimum and to strive to exceed industry or legal standards in protecting private information.
The FTC has been the chief federal agency on privacy policy and enforcement since the 1970s, using enforcement, policy, and education to protect consumers' personal information.
Ethical marketing builds durable trust: the AMA honesty value explicitly rejects approaches that negatively affect trust, and deception trades a lasting relationship for a single transaction.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The AMA Statement of Ethics lists different ethical values across editions: earlier versions named fairness and respect; the current version (read live 2026-08-22) names honesty, responsibility, equity, transparency, and citizenship, with fairness appearing inside the integrity norm.
positions: Earlier AMA statements list fairness and respect as core values
The current AMA Statement of Ethics lists honesty, responsibility, equity, transparency, and citizenship as ethical values
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the current statement read live, and describes fairness as an underlying principle without asserting an outdated value list.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the FTC deception standard turns on the literal truth of individual statements or on the overall impression an ad creates.
positions: Some summaries emphasize the literal truth of each statement
The FTC's own phrasing — ads must be truthful AND not misleading — treats the overall impression as part of the test
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the standard in the FTC's own terms (truthful and not misleading) and notes that an ad can mislead through its overall impression, without inventing legal-test language.

sourceRecords.title: AMA Statement of Ethics (Ethical Norms and Values for Marketers)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A standards body, read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22 (the older /statement-of-ethics/ URL now 404s; the live URL was found via the AMA site's search API). Supports: the ethical norms do no harm / foster integrity / embrace ethical values; the ethical values honesty, responsibility, equity, transparency, and citizenship; honesty as rejecting manipulation, coercion, and approaches that negatively affect trust; equity as recognizing the needs of vulnerable market segments; responsibility as striving to exceed industry or legal standards in protecting private information; and the instruction that marketers must at a minimum adhere to all applicable laws and regulations. Proprietary web content: paraphrased with attribution, no text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Advertising and Marketing (business guidance)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Registry record reused with an identical URL (verified 2026-08-21 by a parallel worker). States that under the law, claims in advertisements must be truthful, cannot be deceptive or unfair, and must be evidence-based. Supports the truthfulness claim. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Advertisement Endorsements (Truth In Advertising topic page)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A, read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-22. Supports: endorsements must be truthful and not misleading; the FTC's Guides Concerning the Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising advise that unrepresentative testimonials may mislead unless accompanied by typical-results information; a material connection between endorser and marketer should be disclosed; the Guides are not regulations, but noncompliance can trigger an FTC Act investigation. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Protecting Consumer Privacy and Security (topic page)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A, read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-22. States the FTC has been the chief federal agency on privacy policy and enforcement since the 1970s, beginning with the Fair Credit Reporting Act, and uses law enforcement, policy initiatives, and consumer and business education to protect consumers' personal information. Also lists COPPA (kids' privacy) under its privacy topics. Supports the privacy framing in the gray-zones section. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Truth In Advertising (topic page)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A, read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-22. Backbone source for the truthfulness section: federal law requires an ad to be truthful, not misleading, and, when appropriate, backed by scientific evidence; the FTC enforces these truth-in-advertising laws and applies the same standards no matter where an ad appears; the FTC looks especially closely at claims that can affect consumers' health or their pocketbooks. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing, Section 5.7: Ethical Concerns and Target Marketing
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A backbone text. openstax.org blocks direct fetch; the canonical section URL was read via a Wayback Machine capture (web.archive.org/web/2025id_/...) on 2026-08-22. Supports: ethics as the systematic study of morality; the AMA Statement of Ethics as the code marketers are expected to follow; morally responsible marketers empathizing with consumers' legitimate needs and wants; children under about 7 or 8 not being able to discern the persuasive intent of advertising (attributed there to the American Psychological Association); older adults exploited with health claims; low-income consumers targeted with high-APR credit and similar schemes; and the notion of companies with a conscience. Paraphrased with attribution; no text reproduced at length.
